pages.title: Where am I?
pages.text:
This page follows your game: it reads your §ladvancements§r (L key) and checks off the Journey steps you have done.

• The §lcurrent age§r is the first one with steps left; its bar shows how far you are.
• §lNext step§r: click it to open its page, with what to make, where and with what.
• The next ages stay gray until you get there.

Each step checks itself off when its goal is reached (an item in your inventory, or a machine running); the next step is also shown §lon screen§r (next page to set it up). Nothing is locked: you can read any page at any time.

pages.title: On-screen display
pages.text:
The Journey's §lnext step§r is shown on screen while you play: its title, its icon and the items gathered (items of its page in your inventory). It hides when a screen is open; “Step done” shows when you finish one.

• §lJ§r key: opens the step's page. §lShift + J§r: its recipe in JEI (if JEI is installed).
• Click the settings above: show or hide, position (top center by default, or a corner), number of steps (1 to 3), size.
• §lLook card§r (what you aim at: crop, machine, animal…): its corner (bottom right by default) and its size (60 to 125%); it moves aside on its own so as not to cover the hotbar, the minimap or the effects, and wraps instead of cutting a text.

Settings are kept on your computer (client config file).

pages.title: Welcome to Pioneer's
How to read this guide
pages.text:
The guide has four parts, in the table of contents on the left:
• §6Getting started§r: this part.
• §6The Journey§r: one chapter per age, in the real order of the game. Each opens with “Goal of this age”, then §lnumbered steps§r: what to make, where, with what. Follow them in order.
• §6Mechanics§r: each system explained once (rotation, steam, foundry, multiblocks, cables, energy…), to reread when a machine does not do what you expect.
• §6Appendices§r: tables and glossary.

§6On a page§r: the §llinks§r under the diagram open the page they name; click an §licon§r to see its recipes in JEI (right-click: its uses); in diagrams, gold-framed boxes unlock what comes next.

§6Navigation§r: mouse wheel to scroll, ← → previous or next page, ↑ ↓ chapter, Ctrl + F to search (accents and capitals do not matter).

pages.title: Your first minutes
pages.text:
1. §lLogs§r by hand, planks, sticks, crafting table.
2. Break §lgravel§r: flint. §lTall grass§r: plant fiber.
3. §lToolmaker's bench§r (2 flint, 3 logs, 3 planks): flint knife, pickaxe and axe.
4. §lFire starter§r (3 sticks, 2 fiber) and a §lcharcoal pit§r: charcoal, then a campfire.
5. Some stone and a furnace: smooth stone and bricks; then the mason's, carpenter's and potter's benches.

Your first machine will be the §lshaking sifter§r with a hand crank, which sifts gravel on its own. The millstone comes later: it needs iron from your first castings.

Step by step from here: “The Journey”, chapter “Primitive Age”.

pages.title: Mod keys
JEI and recipes
pages.text:
§6JEI§r shows every recipe in the mod, including benches, machines, multiblocks, smithing, cooking and world productions.
• §lR§r on an item: how to get it; §lU§r: what it is used for.
• At the bottom of a recipe: the tier required (MKI to MKIV), energy, and the research needed (green once done).
• The “§lMultiblocks§r” category shows each structure in 3D, layer by layer, with a block count.
• In a machine, the arrow opens its recipes; a recipe's “+” locks it into the §lrecipe selector§r.

From this guide, click an icon: JEI opens on its recipes.

pages.title: Handy controls
pages.text:
• §lShift + right-click, empty hand, on a controller§r (multiblock, firebox, drill, blast furnace): shows the blueprint; click again for the next variant, then to hide it.
• §lWrench on a cable§r: the targeted side goes neutral → input → output → off.
• §lWrench on a multiblock port§r: input ↔ output, nothing else: the port sorts each resource by itself (an open stack first, one tank per fluid, cooling first) and an output ejects to its neighbors on its own.
• §lShift + right-click with the wrench§r on a mechanical part: speed, torque, network load.
• §lUpgrade kit§r: right-click a placed machine or buffer, nothing is lost.
• §lCollier pole§r on a pile: progress, leaks, yield.
• §lSeismograph§r: fluid deposit under your feet or direction of the nearest.
• §lComparator§r against a controller: a tank's fill level, or 15 while the machine runs.
• §lShift + right-click with a pneumatic tool§r on a block holding compressed air: refill.

pages.title: The Field Notebook
pages.text:
The first thing this world gives you is not a tool but a book. At the end of the §6initiation§r you receive the §6Field Notebook§r: your name, your vocation, your skills, what you have read, what you have done.

• §lJ§r (or right-click with it in hand) opens it anywhere. The item is only a book: the profile lives in the world, not in the paper.
• Lost, it is made again at the §6Carpenter's Bench§r: 4 paper and 1 leather, with a knife.
• Your character belongs to this world: another world, another notebook.

It remembers what you do, not what you promise. Details: the “Mechanics: The pioneer” chapter.

pages.title: Minimap and waypoints
pages.text:
The §lminimap§r shows the surface you have seen (nothing more: the rest stays dark), with relief shading and water. It remembers what you explored, per world and per dimension.
• §6Keys§r: §bY§r show / hide, §bN§r full-screen map, §bI§r waypoint at your position, §b=§r and §b-§r zoom (change them in Controls).
• §6Layers§r: clan territories (yours, allies, other clans, enemies outlined in red, disputed areas blinking), railroad tracks, stations and harbors, sea routes, robotic roads, hubs and relays, logistics points, entities, players (in their clan color) and members of your clan who are far away.
• §6Waypoints§r: name, color, icon, shown or hidden, on-screen marker with the name and the distance, §lvisible in every situation§r (underground, behind a hill, under water: dimmed when the terrain hides it; off screen, it stays at the edge with an arrow), and in Beacon mode a beam in the world; right-click the full-screen map to place one; a death point is placed automatically. Teleporting (the waypoint's “Teleport” button, “TP” in the list): admins (operators) only, in creative or spectator mode, never in survival or adventure; you arrive at the waypoint's height if it is safe, otherwise on the surface (in the Nether, under the roof), never in a liquid or underground.
• §6Settings§r: button on the full-screen map. Size, corner, square or round shape, scale, rotation with you, opacity, steel or tier trim, text, each layer, entity filters, colors.
In the Nether, the map shows the first floor below the ceiling (or hides itself, your choice).

pages.title: Playing as a party
pages.text:
A §6party§r shares §lJourney progress§r between friends, with no link to clans. Guide (H), §lParty§r button at the top:
• §lInvite§r: the name of an online player; the invitation lasts 10 minutes. They §laccept§r or §ldecline§r from their guide (or /party accept, /party decline). 8 members at most; a player is in one party only.
• §lOn joining§r, progress is merged: everyone gets the Journey steps the others have done.
• §lAfterwards§r, a step done by one member is checked for all; an absent member gets it when they log in.
• §lOn leaving§r (“Leave the party”), you keep everything you have; the party dissolves when only one member is left.
• Everyone gets the step (and its reward, if any) §lonce only§r.
Fallback commands: /party (members and steps), /party invite <player>, /party accept, /party decline, /party leave, /party sync (shares progress again).

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r gear up without a single ore: the hand crank and the shaking sifter (your first machine), flint tools, fire, stone, clay, then your first metal, cast by hand and forged.

§6You need§r a patch of forest near a river (water is only infinite in rivers and oceans), gravel, clay, and a few animals for leather.

§6You unlock§r copper, tin, bronze and iron ingots, forged tools, and the metalworker's bench: what you need for the machines of the Mechanical Age.

§6Good to know§r: there are no ores underground anymore, anywhere. Metal is sifted out of gravel and sand, then melted in a crucible. Tools are no longer made in the crafting grid but at benches.

pages.title: Step 1: wood, flint and fiber
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Chop a few trees by hand: logs → planks and sticks, then the crafting table (grid).
2. Break §lgravel§r: it sometimes drops §lflint§r. You need a dozen or so.
3. Break §ltall grass§r: it sometimes drops a §lplant fiber§r. Keep 5 or 6 (bindings, fire starter).
4. Spot clay at the bottom of water, and sand: you will need them from step 5.

§6Why§r: flint, sticks and fiber make all your first tools. Leather (cows) or string (spiders) can replace fiber as a binding.

pages.title: Step 2: the hand crank and the shaking sifter
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lhand crank§r (1 flint, 2 sticks, 1 plank), §lwooden shafts§r (2 logs → 6), §lcogwheel§r (4 sticks, 4 planks) and §lcogs§r.
2. Grid: §lfiber mesh§r (4 sticks, 5 fiber), then the §lshaking sifter§r (4 sticks, mesh, 2 planks, 1 shaft).
3. Connect the crank to the sifter with a shaft. The crank is weak (~90 W): go through a cogwheel and a cog set diagonally to gear it down.
4. Pour gravel and sand into the sifter (its rope screen is built in, no separate filter): fragments come out on their own.

§6More power§r: a §lwater wheel§r (4 planks, 4 sticks, 1 shaft) in flowing water, or a §lhorse mill§r (cogwheel, 3 logs, shaft) with an animal on a lead, replace the crank.

§6Why§r: it is your first real machine, and the most useful: all the Primitive Age metal comes out of it.

pages.title: Step 3: the toolmaker's bench and flint tools
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §ltoolmaker's bench§r = 2 flint, 3 logs, 3 planks.
2. At the toolmaker's bench, with no tool, §lknap§r the heads: knife blade (1 flint), pickaxe, axe, shovel head (2 flint), saw blade.
3. Still at the toolmaker's bench: head + stick + binding (fiber, string or leather) → §lflint knife, pickaxe, axe, saw§r.

§6Priorities§r: the knife (fiber far more often, and it is a workshop tool), the pickaxe (stone, outcrops), the axe (it fells the whole tree), the saw (planks and slabs at the carpenter's bench).

§6Watch out§r: flint wears out fast. Keep spare flint.

pages.title: Step 4: fire and charcoal
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lfire starter§r = 3 sticks + 2 plant fibers (32 uses, hold right-click for 2 s).
2. §lCharcoal pit§r: a solid block of logs (at least 3 × 3 × 2, 18 logs), fully covered with dirt, one single opening on the bottom row. Light it through the opening and wait until the smoke is gone (2 min + 6 s per log). Break it: 2 to 4 §lcharcoal§r per log.
3. Grid: §lcampfire§r = charcoal + logs + sticks.

§6Faster§r: a §lcoal seam outcrop§r (black block on the surface, pickaxe) gives coal right away.

§6Why§r: the campfire fires the crucible, and charcoal feeds the furnace, the forge hearth and the whole foundry.

pages.title: Step 5: stone and the furnace
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Flint pickaxe: §lstone§r (cobblestone).
2. Grid: the vanilla §lfurnace§r (8 cobblestone). Smelt cobblestone into stone, then stone into §lsmooth stone§r; clay into §lbricks§r.
3. At the toolmaker's bench: §lstone hammer§r (2 cobblestone, 1 stick, 1 binding) and §lstone mortar§r (3 cobblestone, 1 stick).

§6Why§r: smooth stone and bricks open the mason's and potter's benches and the pottery kiln. The hammer and mortar are workshop tools: they go in a bench's tool slots and lose one point per piece.

§6Watch out§r: in Pioneer's the furnace does not melt metal: metal goes through the crucible (step 9).

pages.title: Step 6: finding metal
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. The §lshaking sifter§r from step 2: pour gravel or sand into it, fragments come out on their own. (The §lhand sieve§r of step 7 does the same by hand: fiber mesh, gravel, right-click empty-handed.)
2. Where to look: gravel (copper and iron: malachite, magnetite, hematite), sand (tin and copper: cassiterite, malachite), black sand on beaches (tin and iron), alluvial gravel in rivers or crushed tuff (copper and tin, lots of gold), red sand (hematite).
3. Also break the colored §loutcrops§r on the surface (pickaxe): 1 or 2 fragments each.
4. Grid: 4 fragments → 1 §lraw ore§r (malachite → copper, cassiterite → tin, magnetite and hematite → iron).

§6In bulk§r: a §lwater wheel§r on the shaking sifter keeps it turning day and night.

pages.title: Step 7: carpenter and mason
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lcarpenter's bench§r = 2 sticks, 1 knife, 3 planks, 2 logs. With the saw: §lwooden slabs§r (3 planks → 6); with the knife: fiber (grass, vines, sugar cane), §lfiber rope§r (6 fiber → 2).
2. Grid: §lhand sieve§r (4 sticks, 3 slabs) and §lfiber mesh§r (4 sticks, 5 fiber).
3. Grid: §lmason's bench§r = 2 mortars, 4 smooth stone, 2 cobblestone. With the hammer: §lsmooth stone slab§r; with the mortar: §lfire clay§r (2 clay + 2 sand).

§6Why§r: the hand sieve shakes faster than the crank (step 6); the smooth stone slab and fire clay open the potter and the crucible (step 8).

pages.title: Step 8: clay: the potter and the kiln
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lpotter's bench§r = 2 clay, 1 smooth stone slab, 3 planks, 2 logs.
2. Grid: §lpottery kiln§r = 5 bricks, 2 smooth stone, 1 campfire: it is the kiln's door. Build its §lstructure§r around it (Shift + right-click the door with an empty hand: the blueprint): a 3 × 3 floor of §lbricks§r, the chamber closed with §lbrick stairs§r, a §lbrick slab§r on the front and a brick flue at the back (12 bricks, 7 stairs, 1 slab, at the mason). Once formed, it burns any fuel.
3. At the potter (knife): §lunfired molds§r (ingot: 2 clay; also nugget, plate, rod, gear) and the §lunfired crucible§r (4 fire clay).
4. Fire the molds in the pottery kiln (650 °C). Put the unfired crucible §lon the campfire§r: it becomes the §lclay crucible§r (30 s).

§6Why§r: the clay crucible melts metal over the fire, the molds give it its shape. A mold lasts 128 casts.

§6Note§r: an unfired crucible fired in the pottery kiln gives a §lcrucible§r: it is used by the forge hearth (step 10) and the crucible furnace (Bronze Age).

pages.title: Step 9: the first cast
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. At the toolmaker's bench (knife): §lcrucible tongs§r = 2 sticks, 2 bindings, 1 leather.
2. Set the clay crucible on a lit campfire and feed it raw ore (right-click): it melts. Charcoal at its foot: +100 °C.
3. Place a fired mold on the ground (like a block). Tongs: right-click the crucible, then the mold. Wait for the piece to set and take it empty-handed: your first §lingot§r.
4. Copper (1,085 °C), tin, gold, lead and zinc melt over the fire alone. §lIron§r (1,538 °C) needs a §lhand bellows§r (grid: 4 planks, 2 leather, 1 stick) against the fire: click it steadily.
5. Copper and tin together (3 to 1): §lbronze§r.

§6Aim for§r: §lten iron ingots§r (the first anvil, made of iron), then copper and a little tin. The plate mold and rod mold give plates and rods directly.

pages.title: Step 10: forging your tools
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lforge hearth§r (2 bricks, 1 clay, 1 fired crucible, 5 cobblestone).
2. The anvil is cast: at the potter (knife), an §lunfired anvil mold§r (8 clay), fired in the pottery kiln or on a campfire. Place it on the ground and pour §l10 molten iron ingots§r (1,440 mB: iron melted in the clay crucible with the bellows) into it with the tongs, in several pours. Once it has set, take the first anvil, the §liron anvil§r, empty-handed: it forges every metal, from copper to steel.
3. Hearth with charcoal: an ingot placed on it becomes §lheated metal§r. Hold the tongs in your other hand (it burns). Shift + right-click opens its screen: set how many ingots and how much charcoal it takes.
4. Heated metal on the anvil, hammer in hand: the smithing screen. Pick the shape (pickaxe head, axe head, blade…), strike, draw out, cut until it matches the ghost.
5. Quench the hot piece in water, then at the toolmaker's bench: head + handle + binding. Copper then bronze tools last far longer than flint.
6. Grid: §lmetalworker's bench§r = 2 hammers, 1 copper ingot, 3 planks, 2 logs.

§6Next§r: with iron plates and rods, the whole Mechanical Age opens up.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r spin drive shafts so machines work for you: sifting, milling, crushing, sawing, turning.

§6You need§r wood to start, then the §liron you cast§r in the Primitive Age: iron plates, rods and ingots. The wooden machines (crank, shaking sifter, water wheel, horse mill) were already built in the Primitive Age: here everything needs iron.

§6You unlock§r dust, gravel and sand in bulk, planks and shafts by machine, the wooden fluid buffer and the §lbeam engine§r, the first steam machine.

§6Watch out§r: the §lmillstone is not a first machine§r: it needs a hopper (5 iron plates). Start with the wood lathe and the iron parts.

pages.title: Step 1: iron parts
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lwood lathe§r = 1 iron ingot, 3 sticks, 2 logs, 1 shaft. It turns wooden shafts (8 per log) and metal rods.
2. Cast iron §lplates§r and §lrods§r (plate and rod molds), or forge them.
3. Grid: §liron shaft§r (3 rods → 4) and §liron flywheel§r (8 plates + 1 iron shaft).

§6Why§r: iron shafts and flywheels hold 12,000 N·m (wood breaks at 3,000): they carry the big machines.

pages.title: Step 2: more power
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lWater wheel§r and §lhorse mill§r (Primitive Age, step 2): a drop on one side of the wheel is worth 2.5 times more.
2. §lWindmill§r: hub (2 iron nuggets, cogwheel, 3 planks) + 4 or 8 canvas or plank sails, high up and unobstructed: 1 to 20 kW depending on altitude and weather.
3. Gearboxes and cogwheels to get where you need; Shift + right-click with a wrench reads speed, torque and load.

§6Why§r: the millstone, the crusher and the saw need a lot of torque: a hand crank is not enough.

pages.title: Step 3: the bellows and the wooden buffer
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lforge bellows§r (5 planks, 3 leather, 1 shaft), driven by a shaft and facing a hearth, a furnace or a smelter: twice as hot and as fast.
2. Grid: §lwooden fluid buffer§r = 6 planks, 1 iron ingot, 1 wooden slab. A small barrel of staves with iron hoops: 8,000 mB of cold fluid (water, creosote…), bucket or cable, comparator.
3. Placed on a §lnoria§r, it connects to it and collects the water it lifts.
4. Rings and springs are made on the §lwood lathe§r.

§6Why§r: the bellows will serve the blast furnace; the buffer stores water for boilers and quenching.

pages.title: Step 4: millstone, crusher and saw
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Metalworker's bench (hammer): a §lhopper§r = 5 iron plates + 1 chest.
2. Grid: §lmillstone§r = hopper, 3 smooth stone, 2 planks, 1 shaft (the shaft enters from below or above). Flour, bone meal, flint dust, dyes, metal dusts.
3. Grid: §ljaw crusher§r (4 iron plates, flywheel, iron shaft, 3 smooth stone): stone → gravel → sand, raw ore → crushed ore. 480 N·m.
4. Grid: §lmechanical saw§r (3 slabs, 2 iron plates, iron shaft, 2 logs): 6 planks per log. §lMechanical drill§r: endless stone.

§6Why§r: the crusher doubles your ore, the millstone makes the dusts of Bronze Age recipes.

pages.title: Step 5: water, ropes and wooden cables
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lwinch§r (4 planks, 2 shafts, 3 ropes). Over water it is a well (1,000 mB per trip); over a chest, a lift.
2. §lNoria§r (4 buckets + water wheel): lifts water from a source.
3. Carpenter (saw): §lwooden logistic cable§r = 3 planks + 1 iron ring → 6. It carries items and cold fluids; right-click it: the network diagram.
4. §lWooden hopper§r: no inventory, it passes one item from above to its spout.

§6Why§r: water everywhere (boilers, quenching, cooking) and your first machines linked together.

pages.title: Step 6: the beam engine
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lbeam engine§r = 2 blocks of copper (18 ingots), 1 iron flywheel, 1 iron rod, 1 log, 1 furnace, 3 brick blocks.
2. Fill it with water (bucket or cable) and fuel, wait for the boil.
3. Shaft on the left side, under the flywheel: up to 9,000 N·m at start-up, enough to drive a row of crushers and saws.

§6Why§r: it is the power of the late Mechanical Age, and the first steam. Next come the boiler and steam engine of the Bronze Age.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r mass-produce metal, build a boiler and a steam factory, find your ore deposits and drill them, then make §lsteel§r.

§6You need§r copper, tin and iron ingots, plates and rods (Primitive Age), a metalworker's bench and power (Mechanical Age), plenty of charcoal and fire clay.

§6You unlock§r steel (wrench, industrial benches), ore in quantity, steam everywhere by cable, and, on the side, primitive plastic from resin taps.

§6Shortcut§r: §lruins§r hide scrap; taken apart at the metalworker's bench, it gives steel nuggets long before the blast furnace.

pages.title: Step 1: coppersmith and mass casting
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lcoppersmith's bench§r = 2 copper plates, 1 hammer, 3 planks, 2 logs. It makes rivets, boiler shells, bronze cables, tuyeres.
2. Potter: unfired fire bricks (2 fire clay), fired in the kiln → §lfire bricks§r.
3. Grid: §lcrucible furnace§r (1 copper ingot, 6 fire bricks, 1 brick) with a fired crucible inside, and against it, on any side, a §lcasting table§r (5 smooth stone slabs, 2 copper ingots) holding a mold: it connects by itself.
4. Load metal and fuel; a bellows facing it reaches 1,600 °C. The “Auto” button: it pours into the table on its own.

§6Why§r: 9 ingots per batch instead of 2, and no more tongs.

pages.title: Step 2: alloys
pages.text:
§6To do§r
Mix metals in the crucible or the furnace: the screen shows the composition.
• §lBronze§r: 3 copper to 1 tin (70 to 80% copper): gears, plates, bronze cables, tools.
• §lBrass§r: 3 copper to 1 zinc (70 to 80% copper; raw zinc from sphalerite outcrops, or from the drill): steam dome, valves, gauges, brass wrench.
• §lSolder§r: 3 tin to 2 lead (55 to 65% tin; raw lead from galena outcrops): solder wire for circuits.

§6Wrong dose?§r Nothing is lost: the forge pours as much alloy as it can and keeps the surplus (screen: “Pours: bronze 4 ingots · left: tin 144 mB”), which then pours by itself. At the crucible furnace, pick the alloy in the §lRecipe§r slot: it only takes what it needs and the rest waits in its slot.

pages.title: Step 3: the boiler
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lboiler firebox§r (2 iron plates, 1 copper plate, 1 furnace, 5 fire bricks), on the ground: it is the controller, in the middle of the front.
2. Build the structure from the blueprint (Shift + right-click the firebox with an empty hand): behind it, 4 §lfire brick fireboxes§r in a cross; above, two levels of 5 §lcopper boiler shells§r (6 copper plates, 8 rivets) in a cross, one more shell in the center and the §lsteam dome§r (brass and copper plates, rivets) in front of it; an optional §lwater gauge§r on the side.
3. Mason: §lchimney§r (4 bricks + 1 iron plate) on the top shell, 1 to 8 blocks: the taller it is, the better the draft.
4. Water (bucket or cable), charcoal in the firebox: the fire catches by itself (“Fire: on” button in the interface); the screen reads “Heating”, then “Making steam”.

§6Watch out§r: steam blows nothing up (with the reserve full, the fire keeps going and the surplus escapes), but a boiler fired §lwithout water§r explodes: keep it filled, and fit a §lboiler low-water cutoff§r (coppersmith): below 20% water, it shuts the firebox down.

pages.title: Step 4: steam engine and bronze cable
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Coppersmith: §lbronze logistic cable§r (2 bronze plates, 1 bronze ring → 4). It carries steam (gas channel) and everything else.
2. Grid: §lsteam engine§r (2 bronze plates, 1 bronze cable, 2 iron rods, 1 flywheel, 3 iron plates).
3. Connect the dome to the engine with the cable. Steam in from the back or bottom, shaft on the sides: 12,000 N·m, 120 rpm unloaded, 0.48 mB/t of steam per rpm.
4. Spent steam leaves through the exhaust (front): keep the boiler filled (bronze cable from a water supply, or a bucket).

§6Why§r: the unlimited power of this age, and soon electricity (dynamo, Industrial Age).

pages.title: Step 5: the steam factory
Step 6: prospecting and drilling
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Forge a copper prospector's hammer head; at the toolmaker's bench: the §lprospector's hammer§r.
2. Right-click the ground: direction and distance of the nearest deposit; on the spot, its ore and reserve. Colored outcrops give it away too.
3. Grid: §lsteam drill§r (bronze plates and gears, bronze cable, steam engine, bronze pickaxe head). It is a front base: around it, 7 §lbases§r including one §ldrill port§r (steam and output), in the center the §lbronze drill string§r (4 stacked blocks), around it 3 levels of §lderricks§r in a cross, then 2 derricks on top and the §lcrown block§r. Shift + right-click empty-handed: the blueprint.
4. With 24 mB/t of steam: one raw ore every 3 s, until the deposit runs dry.

§6Limit§r: the steam drill only works level 1 deposits (iron, copper, tin, lead, zinc, gold, coal, and §lredstone§r: desert, badlands, plains). Redstone only comes from drills: grind its ore in the §lsteam macerator§r (4 dust); it makes the red alloy and the redsteel of the induction furnace.

pages.title: Step 7: the blast furnace and steel
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Mason: §lfire bricks§r as blocks (4 bricks + 1 fire clay). Coppersmith: §ltuyeres§r. Grid: §lprimitive blast furnace§r (7 fire bricks, 1 iron plate, 1 crucible): it is the tap hole.
2. Build the tower from the blueprint (Shift + right-click empty-handed on the controller): a round base of §lfire brick fireboxes§r (the tap hole in the middle of the front, §lone tuyere§r in the middle of the back), then a fire brick tower tapering into a chimney, hollow in the middle.
3. Blow air: a bellows behind the tuyere, facing it (it takes wind to pass 1,500 °C), or a steam blower.
4. Load from the top: iron (ore, crushed, ingots), charcoal, §lquicklime§r (calcite fired in the pottery kiln). Above 1,500 °C, §lsteel§r flows.

§6Watch out§r: without lime, a quarter goes to slag. Steel does not melt in a crucible.

pages.title: Step 8: ruins and resin: getting ready for industry
pages.text:
§6Ruins§r: sites of derelict machines, guarded by Sentinels. Break the derelict blocks: §lscrap§r. At the metalworker's bench, with a hammer, 1 MKI scrap → 2 §lsteel nuggets§r.

§6Resin§r (start early, it flows slowly):
1. Carpenter: §lwooden resin tap§r, placed on the side of a living spruce (at least 3 logs, leaves on top) → §lraw resin§r.
2. Pottery kiln: resin → §lrosin§r. Mason (mortar): rosin + sawdust + fiber → mix; in the kiln: §lprimitive plastic§r.
3. On a §ljungle§r tree, the same tap gives §lraw latex§r; the §lsteam extractor§r turns it into §lnatural rubber§r, and resin into §lresin glue§r (machine only).

§6Why§r: steel opens the industrial benches; primitive plastic makes, at the steam press, the perforated board of the first circuit; natural rubber sheathes the MKI logistic cable.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r move from steam to electricity: industrial benches, the vacuum tube circuit and the MKI machine hull, your first power (dynamo, then solid combustion generator), iron by machine (crusher, crucible, casting), MKI workshop machines, your first multiblock, the drill and level 2 ores, then silver and components by machine.

§6You need§r plenty of steel (blast furnace or ruins), copper, brass, bronze, primitive plastic, and a running boiler or steam engine.

§6You unlock§r the §lfour tiers§r of machines (MKI to MKIV), level 2 ores (bauxite, nickel, chromium) and the MKI circuit: the door to the Chemical Age.

§6The tier rule§r: every workshop machine exists as MKI, MKII, MKIII, MKIV (×2 speed, ×4 energy per tier) and as an industrial multiblock; each one starts from the §lmachine hull§r of its tier. An MKII recipe needs at least an MKII machine, and an MKI machine never takes a part of a higher tier.

pages.title: Step 1: the wrench and the industrial benches
Step 2: the coke oven
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Assembly bench (wrench): §lcoke oven§r (8 fire bricks): it is the door. Build its structure around it (Shift + right-click with an empty hand: the blueprint): a floor of 7 §lfire brick fireboxes§r with a §ltuyere§r in the middle of the back, then a chamber of §lfire bricks§r (21 blocks), hollow in the middle.
2. Coke oven: coal → §lcoke§r with no fuel, plus §lcreosote§r; logs → §lcharcoal§r and creosote. Coal tar and coke oven gas will come from the §lpyrolysis oven§r.
3. Steel tools are forged by hand on the iron anvil. §lTempered steel§r comes later from the §lindustrial power hammer (hot forging)§r (a multiblock whose core is a forge hearth): glowing bloom, then quench.

§6Why§r: coke replaces charcoal across industrial metallurgy.

pages.title: Step 3: the vacuum tube circuit and the MKI machine hull
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Redstoner bench (file): §lvacuum tubes§r, §lcarbon resistors§r (a §lcoal ball§r from the steam compressor, copper wire, porcelain), §lpaper capacitors§r, §lrelays§r (copper coil, bronze spring, a §lred alloy wire§r, porcelain); steam press: §lperforated board§r (2 primitive plastic → 4).
2. Advanced components bench (wrench): the §lvacuum tube circuit§r (MKI), the §lsteel machine frame§r (steel plates, rods, and steel screws and bolts from the steam lathe), §lbearings§r (steel balls from the lathe).
3. Assembly bench (wrench): the §lMKI machine hull§r = steel frame + vacuum tube circuit + 2 brass plates and 2 brass rods. Nothing electric, but everything goes through the Bronze Age: §lred alloy§r (steam induction furnace: 1 copper + 2 redstone from the steam drill), drawn into wire at the lathe then the steam wiremill, the compressor, the rolling mill and the steam press.

§6Why§r: every MKI machine = MKI machine hull + 2 to 4 parts of its trade (guide: “Machine hulls”).

pages.title: Step 4: your first power
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. To get started: the §lCompact Dynamo MKI§r (assembly bench: MKI machine hull, copper coil and ring, bronze gear, 2 bearings) on the §lsteam engine§r's shaft: 1 J = 1 FE, up to 2,048 FE/t.
2. Right after: the §lMKI Solid Combustion Generator§r (MKI machine hull, 2 fire bricks, copper coil, iron wire mesh, steel pipe). It burns coal, coke, charcoal, wood, pellets: §l2,048 FE/t§r; one coal = 3.28 MFE.
3. §lLogistic cable MKI§r: it carries energy (and items, fluids, gases, data).
4. Later: the §lliquid combustion generator§r (diesel, ethanol, oils) and the §lgas turbine§r (natural gas, biogas, wood gas…), MKI to MKIV and as multiblocks.

§6Rule of thumb§r: an MKI machine draws about 1,024 FE/t while running: one MKI solid generator runs two of them.

pages.title: Step 5: iron at MKI: crusher, crucible and casting
pages.text:
§6To do§r at the assembly bench (wrench), right from your first power (each one on an MKI machine hull):
1. §lMKI crusher§r: 1 raw ore → §l2 crushed ores§r. Crushing doubles the metal.
2. §lCompact Industrial Crucible MKI§r: it melts ore §l×1.5§r (one crushed or raw ore = 216 mB), dust at 144 mB (one ingot) and fragments at 36 mB.
3. §lCompact Casting Machine MKI§r with its §lingot die§r: molten metal → ingots (and a few nuggets).
4. Link the three with cables (items, fluids): §l3 ingots per ore§r, no coke, no pig iron (4, 5 then 6 at the next tiers). Same for copper, tin, lead, zinc and gold. Simpler: the §lindustrial furnace§r smelts ore (1 ingot, 2 if crushed), in §l4 s§r at MKI, 2 s at MKII, 1 s at MKIII and 0.5 s at MKIV.

§6Rule of thumb§r: one MKI line makes about 8 ingots a minute, 15 with water-cooled casting; at MKII everything runs twice as fast. Steel is only made in the §lblast furnace§r (the primitive one, then the industrial blast furnace that refines its own pig iron): no crucible, converter or arc furnace makes it.

pages.title: Step 6: the other workshop machines
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Advanced components bench: the §lelectric motor§r (it already needs power: a machine makes it).
2. Assembly bench: the compact kit's §lindustrial furnace§r and the metallurgy workshop machines: §lcrusher (fine grinding)§r, §lindustrial furnace (roasting)§r, press, wiremill…
3. Plug in energy with a cable; set the sides (tab on the left) and auto-eject.
4. §lRecipe selector§r: the “Recipe” slot locks the machine onto one recipe; it refuses everything else.

§6Watch out§r: “Tier too low: MKII required” = a recipe of a higher tier than the machine.

pages.title: Step 7: your first multiblock
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Assembly bench: §lIndustrial Casing MKI§r (×6), §lindustrial glass§r, ports (items, fluids, gases, energy) and the machine's §lcontroller§r.
2. Shift + right-click empty-handed on the placed controller: the blueprint appears as a ghost. Fill it; the interior stays empty.
3. The multiblock's tier = that of its weakest casing or glass. It runs in parallel (4 at MKI) and heats up: plan for cooling water.

§6JEI§r: the “Multiblocks” page shows each blueprint in 3D and counts the blocks.

pages.title: Step 8: the drill
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Assembly bench: the §ldrill§r controller (it takes a steam drill, an MKI machine hull, a galvanized steel wire rope, a centrifugal pump). Build it from the blueprint on a deposit.
2. It works level 2 deposits: chalcopyrite, pentlandite (nickel), chromite, vanadinite, bauxite, zircon, fluorite, wolframite, ilmenite, pitchblende, lapis…

§6Why§r: the nickel, chromium, aluminum and titanium of the late age all come from there.

pages.title: Step 9: concentrating: flotation and tar
pages.text:
§6The typical path§r of an ore: crusher (×2 crushed) → crusher (fine grinding) → §lflotation§r (concentrate) → §lroasting§r → reduction.
1. The flotation reagent comes from §lpitch§r: the coal tar of the §lpyrolysis oven§r (multiblock: coal → coke, tar and coke oven gas) run through the §lchemical reactor§r, then the §lmixer§r; wood tar from the same oven works too.
2. §lOre Separator (flotation)§r: argentite, pentlandite and bauxite concentrates.
3. Argentite: roasting (oxygen: the hydroponic farm (microalgae) and its microalgae), then the §lindustrial furnace (reduction)§r with coke: §lsilver§r.

§6Why§r: silver makes relays and circuits in the assembler (next step). Each metal has several routes: Metallurgy covers them. Ore processed by machines yields more than ore melted as is (×1.25 to ×2).

pages.title: Step 10: silver and components by machine
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lSilver§r: argentite from the drill (step 8), or silver dust from gold on the ore separator (shaking table), melted and cast.
2. Later, the §lMKI Assembler§r (with chemistry) will make components in bulk, twice as many as a bench: relays (silver foil, primitive plastic), resistors (coke), vacuum tube circuits on an etched board (solder): 2 per recipe.

§6Rule of thumb§r: the circuit opens the seismograph, the induction furnace and chemistry. The dynamo and the solid combustion generator are still enough; liquid combustion generators, the gas turbine and the energy buffer come with chemistry (page “How much each generator makes”).

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r find and pump oil, distill and crack it, make aluminum, rubber and gaskets, plastics, heavy chemicals, electric gear, electronics (chips, MKII circuit), then move to tier MKII (MKII machine hull and casings).

§6You need§r running MKI machines, the MKI circuit, plenty of power (chemistry is hungry), bauxite from the drill.

§6You unlock§r tier MKII: all MKII machines, compact and multiblock, open with the MKII machine hull.

§6On the side§r: the living world (biomass, oils, hydroponic farms) complements oil without replacing it.

pages.title: Step 1: finding and pumping oil
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Grid: §lseismograph§r (steel plates, spyglass, 2 vacuum tube circuits, copper coil). Use it in a desert or on the ocean: it finds oil and gas deposits.
2. On land: a §lpumpjack§r on the deposit (multiblock only: Shift + right-click its controller for the blueprint). At sea: the free-form §loffshore platform§r, with its risers and production tubing.
3. Pressure drops as you pump: inject water to raise it again.

pages.title: Step 2: distilling and cracking
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lDistillation column§r (tower multiblock, MKI casings are enough): crude splits into fixed cuts, one per level of output ports (top to bottom). For a single cut (naphtha, say), the §lcompact distillery§r is enough, slower and without the other fractions.
2. §lIndustrial cracker§r (the Cracker's multiblock, which does steam cracking): naphtha becomes ethylene and propylene, the base of plastics, and §lbutadiene§r, the base of rubber.
3. Store in tanks; corrosive or very cold fluids need advanced cables.

pages.title: Step 3: plastics
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lChemical reactor§r (polymerization): polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PTFE pellets…
2. §lPlastic sheets§r at the rolling mill (calendering), pipes and sheathing at the casting machine or the §lextruder§r.
3. §lPolystyrene foam§r: it goes into the MKII frame.

§6Why§r: plastics and PTFE go into MKII cables, components and electronics.

pages.title: Step 4: the living world at scale
Step 5: aluminum, the MKII metal
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lBauxite§r (level 2 deposit) → Bayer digesters: alumina.
2. §lIndustrial electrolyzer§r (the multiblock; its controller is built with two carbon anodes): alumina, cryolite and carbon anodes → §laluminum§r (Hall-Héroult). With copper: duralumin.
3. Cryolite goes through the chemical reactor. Also get nickel (pentlandite) and chromium (chromite) ready: the stainless steel of the next age.

§6Next§r: tier MKII needs aluminum, duralumin and rubber gaskets (step 6).

pages.title: Step 6: rubber and gaskets
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lSulfur§r: in the chemical reactor, §lcoke oven gas§r from the pyrolysis oven, passed over iron dust (the purifying mass of the old gasworks), leaves its sulfur behind. Lazurite (ore separator) and the Claus process (molten sulfur, solidified in the cryogenic unit (heat exchange)) give more.
2. Basic route: §lnatural rubber§r (raw latex from a resin tap on a §ljungle§r tree, in the steam extractor or the MKI dryer). 3 natural rubber + 1 sulfur in the §lautoclave§r (vulcanization; the MKI autoclave is built with a leather gasket): 1 vulcanized rubber.
3. Petrochemical route, more profitable: chemical reactor, butadiene + water → §llatex§r, with acetic acid → §lsynthetic rubber§r; 2 synthetic + 1 sulfur: §l2§r vulcanized rubber (or the mixer's masterbatch: carbon black, sulfur).
4. At the carpenter's bench, with a knife: §lrubber gaskets§r.

§6Why§r: the gasket is the part of tier MKII.

pages.title: Step 7: heavy chemistry
pages.text:
§6To do§r
• §lElectrolyzer§r (membrane electrolysis): brine → chlorine, caustic soda, hydrogen; brine alone gives chlorine and hydrogen first: lock the caustic soda recipe in the §lRecipes§r tab.
• §lIndustrial gas separator§r (multiblock): air separation (nitrogen, oxygen, argon: cold and inert gases) and raw gas processing.
• Chemical reactor: ammonia (Haber-Bosch, in the multiblock), nitric and sulfuric acids: fertilizer, explosives, reagents for the metal routes.

§6Why§r: most MKII and MKIII metals (titanium, zirconium, niobium) go through these reagents.

pages.title: Step 8: electric gear
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. In the MKI §lAssembler (components)§r: the §lvoltaic cell§r (2 lead-acid batteries, 2 copper coils, MKI circuit, plastic, galvanized sheet).
2. Still in the assembler, with the cell: the §lVoltaic armor§r (21 armor while powered, night vision, speed, softened falls) and its tools: §ldrill§r, §lchainsaw§r, §lhedge trimmer§r, §lshock baton§r.
3. With hydrogen (electrolyzer): the §lhydrogen jetpack§r (hold jump in the air; Z key: hover) and the §lflamethrower§r.
4. Recharge in the slot of an §lenergy buffer§r; hydrogen in the slot of a §lgas buffer§r, or drop a capsule onto the item.

§6Why§r: the gear of this age, before modular gear; the Voltaic pieces will be the base of Graviton.

pages.title: Step 9: electronics
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lSilicon§r (arc or industrial furnace (reduction)), single crystal (crystallizer (crystal pulling)), wafers.
2. Optical engraver, clean room: §ltransistors§r, §lintegrated circuits§r.
3. Pick-and-place machine: the §ltransistor circuit§r (MKII, discrete logic: transistors and diodes), then §lprocessors§r.
4. The transistor circuit goes into the §lMKII machine hull§r and the §lMKII casings§r: next step.

§6Why§r: each circuit generation opens a tier of machines.

pages.title: Step 10: tier MKII
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Advanced components bench: §laluminum machine frame§r (aluminum, duralumin, aluminum fasteners, gasket; the bill of materials goes through chemistry: JEI shows it).
2. Assembly bench: §lIndustrial Casing MKII§r, upgrade kits; the §lMKII machine hull§r (aluminum frame, transistor circuit, electrum plates and rods) is made with the transistor circuit (previous step).
3. Tier 1 metals: the MKII crucible melts ore §l×2§r (4 ingots per crushed ore); then, with the §lMKII extractor (leaching)§r (it needs electronics, step 9), §lacid leaching§r: crushed ore + sulfuric acid → §lelectrolyzer§r → dust → industrial furnace: §l5 ingots per ore§r (6 at MKIII, 7 at MKIV).

§6Why§r: your machines move to MKII (twice as fast) and the big chemistry multiblocks need MKII casings.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r pull uranium out of ore, make stainless steel and titanium (the Kroll reactor is an MKII machine), move on to processors and the MKIII circuit, automate your factories with computing up to the computer, gather the three space milestones, compute and research, build a launch complex and go to the Moon, then enrich the uranium, make fuel and bring a reactor critical.

§6You need§r heavy chemistry (acids, fluorine), the MKII circuit and machine hull, zirconium, plenty of water.

§6You unlock§r megawatts of power, computing (GOPS) and the three §lspace program milestones§r: titanium, kerolox and a programmed flight computer.

§6Careful§r: radiation can be measured and worn; a runaway core melts and explodes.

pages.title: Step 1: protection and uranium
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. A §ldosimeter§r and the hazmat gear (hood, jacket…): dose is measured and builds up.
2. Ore: §lpitchblende§r (level 2 deposits in mountains and snow) or §lmonazite§r (level 2 deposits on beaches and rivers), with the drill.
3. Solvent extraction → §lyellowcake§r.

pages.title: Step 2: stainless steel and titanium
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lStainless steel§r: ferrochrome and ferronickel in the induction furnace (chromium and nickel from level 2 deposits).
2. §lTitanium§r: ilmenite → chlorination (chlorine) → §lKroll reactor§r (magnesium) → sponge → §lindustrial crucible (vacuum)§r (argon).

§6Why§r: stainless steel and titanium make tier MKIII, and titanium is the first of the three space milestones.

pages.title: Step 3: processors and the MKIII circuit
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lMulticore processor§r (fine engraving, packages) on the pick-and-place machine.
2. §lMicrocontroller circuit§r (MKIII).
3. §lTitanium machine frame§r, §lMKIII machine hull§r (frame, microcontroller circuit, chrome) and §lMKIII casings§r.

§6Next§r: nuclear power and computing, which open space.

pages.title: Step 4: computing
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lRelay cabinet§r: 4 simple rules between machines linked with the configurator.
2. §lProgrammable logic controller§r: 16 rules, timers, counters; supervision screens.
3. §lComputer§r: PioScript programs (a simplified Python), floppy disks, links. The MKI logistic cable carries data and compute; the §lnetwork terminal§r shows everything.

pages.title: Step 5: the three space milestones
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lTitanium§r (Kroll reactor, industrial crucible (vacuum)).
2. A §lpropellant plant§r: RP-1 kerosene + liquid oxygen = §lkerolox§r.
3. A §lflight computer§r, programmed by the computer (flight.flash): the §lprogrammed flight computer§r.

§6Why§r: these three milestones open the root of the research tree (K key): the space program begins.

pages.title: Step 6: compute and data centers
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lData center§r: compute (GOPS) shared over the network, for space research and AI.
2. Link it with an MKI or better logistic cable: the digital network carries compute to the research lab (next step).

pages.title: Step 7: research
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lResearch lab§r and §lreceiving antenna§r, linked by the logistic cable (digital network); data banks for the surplus.
2. §lK§r key: the research tree. Each research costs data of one type (orbit, surface, geology…) and compute: data centers supply it.
3. The first data comes from probes (step 9).

pages.title: Step 8: the launch complex
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lLaunch pad core§r surrounded by §llaunch pad§r slabs and a §llaunch tower§r: the disk size sets the tier (green MKI to burgundy MKIV).
2. §lLaunch complex ports§r for propellant and cargo.
3. The §lrocket integration hall§r (multiblock) assembles rockets from their parts.

pages.title: Step 9: the lunar probe
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. A §ltier 1 rocket§r with a §lprobe module§r, kerolox in the tank.
2. “Probe” mission to the Moon from the launch pad core.
3. Lunar data reaches the antenna: research “Moon orbit”, “Space suit”.

pages.title: Step 10: to the Moon
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. A full §lspace suit§r at the equipment assembly table (oxygen reserve full).
2. Tier 1 rocket with a §lcrew cabin module§r, “Crewed” mission: Space to lift off, the map to pick the Moon.
3. On site: low gravity, no air. Mine lunarium and crater ice; bring back lunar rock.

pages.title: Step 11: enrichment and fuel
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Conversion: yellowcake → green salt → uranium hexafluoride (fluorine from heavy chemistry).
2. §lCentrifuge cascade§r (or laser separation): enriched and depleted uranium.
3. §lPellets§r → §lfuel rods§r (zircaloy cladding) → §lfuel assembly§r.

pages.title: Step 12: the fission reactor
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Build the §lFission Reactor Generation I§r from its blueprint: core, control rods, pumps, exchangers.
2. Water in, steam out to the turbines; the §lautopilot§r holds the temperature.
3. Spent (hot) assemblies go to the §lspent fuel pool§r.
4. Then: the §lhot cell§r and the §lhot cell (reprocessing)§r (plutonium, MOX, tritium), then the §lFast Neutron Reactor Generation II§r (sodium), which breeds more fuel than it burns.

§6Watch out§r: above 112% of rated power, the core melts (corium), then explodes.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r bring back from each world the metal of the next tier: lunar alloy first (the launch complex, the probe and the first flight to the Moon are at the end of the Atomic Age).

§6You need§r the T1 rocket and the space suit (Atomic Age), the research lab and data centers, a complete MKIII industry.

§6You unlock§r tier §lMKIV§r (lunar alloy), robotics, bases on other worlds, then T2 to T10 rockets all the way to Pluto.

§6The cycle of a world§r: probe (orbit) → crewed flight (surface) → ores (geology) → plants (biology) → blueprint of the next rocket.

pages.title: Step 1: lunar alloy and tier MKIV
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. §lLunar alloy§r in the industrial crucible (vacuum) (lunarium, titanium aluminide, argon).
2. Lunar alloy plates: §ltungsten machine frame§r, then the §lMKIV machine hull§r (frame, photonic circuit, osmiridium), MKIV casings, ultimate cables.

§6Why§r: MKIV is the last machine tier; each next world brings its metals to rockets and machines.

pages.title: Step 2: settling in
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Pressurized base: closed room, §loxygen diffuser§r, §lairlock doors§r.
2. §lSpace greenhouse§r (plants from other worlds), §lrover garage§r and radar (exotic deposits).
3. Robotic hub and logistic points: drones, robots, rovers and turtles deliver, mine, build (map: O key).
4. Chunk loader, force field against meteors, rocket cargo network.

pages.title: Step 3: world after world to Pluto
pages.text:
§6The cycle§r, world after world: probe → crewed flight → geology → biology → blueprint of the next rocket.
• T2 Mars, Phobos, Deimos (thermal suit); T3 Venus, T4 Mercury (acid suit);
• T5 asteroid belt; T6 moons of Jupiter; T7 Saturn; T8 Uranus; T9 Neptune; T10 Pluto and Charon.

Rockets move to hydrolox (T3), then nuclear (T8). Research needs more and more compute. Charon gives the §lmordorite§r of the Space Stabilizer.

pages.title: Goal of this age
pages.text:
§6You will§r forge a stellar core, prepare simulated planets, visit the gas giants and neighboring stars, hold a star then a black hole in a field globe, and simulate whole galaxies.

§6You need§r tier MKIV, plutonium, deuterium and tritium from nuclear power, mordorite from Charon, and gigawatts.

§6You unlock§r stellar plasma, void singularity, T11 to T13 rockets, stardust, neutronium, dark matter and quasar crystals.

pages.title: Step 1: gravity compressor and stellar core
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. The §lgravity compressor§r: a sphere multiblock, full of graviton coils.
2. Plutonium, deuterium and tritium compressed: the §lstellar core§r.

pages.title: Step 2: simulated planets
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. Gravity compressor: a planet's rocks (or gases) → compacted matter.
2. §lSynthesizer§r: data → empty planet; three gases → proto-planet; stellar plasma → simulated planet.
3. Eight planets to make, one per simulator slot.

pages.title: Step 3: gas giants and neighboring stars
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. T11 rocket and the §latmospheric suit§r: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, landed on an §laerostat§r; a §ldrone bay§r harvests gas pockets.
2. A station around the Sun: the §lsolar absorber§r turns the star into a power plant.
3. Keep the §lmetallic hydrogen§r: with the black hole's void singularity (step 5) and plasma, it will make the §lvoid singularity cells§r, then the void drive.
4. T12: Alpha Centauri; T13 (void drive): TRAPPIST-1.

pages.title: Step 4: the Space Stabilizer
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. An 11 × 11 × 11 globe: casing on the edges, glass or ports elsewhere; at the center of each face, a power port with a field emitter behind it.
2. The controller at the bottom center of a face; put the stellar core in its slot.
3. Ignition: 1 GFE at once, 6 powered emitters. The star turns lava into §lstellar plasma§r.

pages.title: Step 5: the black hole
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. At the compressor: a stellar core and 100,000 mB of stellar plasma → §lsingularity core§r.
2. In the stabilizer it becomes a black hole: water turns into §lvoid singularity§r.
3. Keep it: with plasma and the metallic hydrogen of the gas giants (step 3), it makes the §lvoid singularity cells§r of the void drive.

pages.title: Step 6: the Space Simulator and galaxies
pages.text:
§6To do§r
1. The §lSpace Simulator§r: 25-block globe, 6 rift projectors, ring of supreme coils, controller under the globe.
2. Solar mode: the eight planets produce forever.
3. Galaxy mode: Big Bang (250 GFE, stellar plasma), then spirals, ellipticals, irregulars, quasars: stardust, neutronium, dark matter, quasar crystals.

The end of the road… for now.

pages.title: Workshops
Workshop tools
Flint tools
Tools by tier
pages.text:
Every material has the §lfull set§r: pickaxe, axe, shovel, hoe, sword, prospector's hammer, area tools (mining hammer, excavator, scythe), hammer, file, saw, knife, mortar and wrench (flint keeps its knapped tools). Within a tier you pick a §lprofile§r rather than a “better” metal (durability · speed · damage · enchantability):
§lTier 0§r flint 90 · 3.6 · 0.8 · 4.
§lTier 1§r copper 180 · 7.2 · 1.0 · 12 (fast, fragile); iron 600 · 4.8 · 2.4 · 9 (durable, slow); bronze 450 · 6.4 · 2.0 · 12 (all-round).
§lTier 2§r steel 1,200 · 7.6 · 2.8 · 14; hardened steel 2,000 · 6.4 · 3.4 · 9 (hard, slow); brass 700 · 7.2 · 2.2 · 25 (enchantable).
§lTier 3§r titanium 1,800 · 10.5 · 3.0 · 16 (light); stainless 3,200 · 8.4 · 3.4 · 12 (durable); duralumin 1,100 · 12 · 2.6 · 15 (very fast, fragile); §lgold§r 2,600 · 14 · 3.6 · 30 (precious: very fast, top enchantability).
§lTier 4§r tungsten carbide 5,200 · 9.2 · 6.0 · 8 (hard); vanadium steel 4,400 · 11.2 · 4.6 · 14; stellite 7,000 · 10 · 4.0 · 16 (durable).
§lTier 5§r osmiridium 16,000 · 12 · 6.0 · 14; titanium aluminide 6,000 · 16 · 5.0 · 16 (very fast); nitinol 4,000 · 13 · 5.2 · 18 (§lself-repairing§r, 1 point every 10 s in the inventory).
Mining level: copper 1, iron and bronze 2, tier 2: 3, tiers 3 to 5: 4 (like netherite). Heads are cast (copper, bronze, brass, gold), forged (iron, steels), then turned on the lathe or sintered (carbide) in the Industrial Age. The prospector's hammer probes up to 64 blocks, then 128, 160 and 192 at tiers 3, 4 and 5.

pages.title: Area tools
Metal armor
pages.text:
Armor is §lforged§r at the §6metalworker's bench§r (hammer + file), from the metal's plates (ingots for hardened steel), sometimes with steel screws; vanilla metal armor no longer exists (converted). Defense helmet · chestplate · leggings · boots:
§lbronze§r 2 · 5 · 4 · 1; §liron§r 2 · 6 · 5 · 2; §lsteel§r 3 · 7 · 6 · 2; §lhardened steel§r 3 · 8 · 6 · 3 (heavy); §ltitanium§r 3 · 8 · 6 · 3 (enchantable); §ltungsten carbide§r 4 · 9 · 7 · 3 (the toughest); §lnitinol§r 4 · 9 · 7 · 4 (§lself-repairing§r).
§6Gold§r: heavily reinforced, on par with hardened steel (3 · 8 · 6 · 3), top enchantability (30), and each piece worn removes §l15% of burns and radiation dose§r; piglins stay neutral. §lGold tools§r are tier 3, very fast (see the previous page).

pages.title: The tanner's bench
pages.text:
The §6Tanner's Bench§r works leather, fur and cloth. It §lreplaces Minecraft's loom§r, which can no longer be crafted (village looms stay).
• §lCrafting§r: in the grid, 2 leather, 1 knife, 2 pegs, 1 plank and 2 logs.
• §lTools§r: a §lknife§r and §lshears§r in the tool slots; they wear a little with each piece.
• §lWhat it makes§r: the 80 pieces of the 20 cosmetic outfits and the craftable banner patterns (flower, creeper, skull, Mojang).
• §lPatterns§r: the bench's §lPatterns§r button opens the banner loom (banner, dye, pattern), like the old loom.
Most outfits need wool, canvas, leather and a dye; the outfits of the last ages want the materials of their age (lenses, aluminum foil, aramid fiber, rubber, PVC).

pages.title: Clothes
pages.text:
Your face, beard and hair are your §lskin§r's. The mod §ldresses§r you.
• §lCosmetic panel§r: left of the inventory (E key), 4 slots in line with the armor: headwear, top, bottoms, footwear.
• §lPutting on§r: drop the piece in its slot, §lShift + click§r the piece in the inventory, or right-click with the piece in hand. §lShift + click§r on a slot puts it away.
• §lSwitch§r: the small button left of each slot shows the §lgarment§r (T-shirt) or the §larmor§r (shield). The armor protects either way; headwear with or without a helmet, as you like.
• §lNo protection§r: a garment does not replace armor. It §lnever§r drops on death.
• Other players see you dressed; a client option (§lhideOthersCosmetics§r, §lhideOwnCosmetics§r) hides clothes.
In Creative mode the inventory has no panel: put the piece on with a right-click.

pages.title: The twenty outfits
pages.text:
Each outfit has four pieces; wear them all for the §lDressed to the Nines§r advancement. Nothing forces you to match them.
• §6Primitive and mechanical age§r: Peasant, Blacksmith, Winter.
• §6Bronze and steam§r: Miner, Sailor, Steam Engineer, Alchemist, Explorer, Merchant, Village Guard, Desert, Fisherman.
• §6Industrial age§r: Railwayman, Captain, Evening.
• §6Chemistry and life§r: Chemist, Botanist.
• §6Atom and space§r: Aviator, Retro Astronaut, Nuclear Scientist.
The astronaut's bubble helmet is the only headwear that wraps the head: it is made of glass.

pages.title: Finding metal
The charcoal pit
pages.text:
§lStep by step§r:
1. Stack §llogs§r into a solid box: from 3 × 3 × 2 to 7 × 7 × 4, at least §l18 logs§r, at least 85% full.
2. §lCover it completely§r (top and sides) with dirt, clay, gravel, sand or stone.
3. Leave §la single opening§r, on the §lbottom row§r: one air block against a log.
4. Light that log through the opening (§lflint and steel§r or fire charge). A message confirms the log count and duration; otherwise it says what is wrong (too small, not full, extra openings, marked with particles).
5. Wait: the smoke is §lwhite§r (drying), then §lblue§r (charring), then nearly invisible: done (about 2 min + 6 s per log). Don't block the opening for more than 2 minutes: the pile goes out.

The wood turns into a §6charred log pile§r: break it for 2 to 4 charcoal per log, and some ash. A §lleak§r in the cover lets air in: the wood burns, only §6ash§r is left — and fire may spread. The §6collier pole§r probes progress, leaks and yield.

Under the pile, a §6clay drain§r collects §6creosote§r: a bucket takes it; it tars ropes and burns long.

pages.title: The metal loop
pages.text:
Metal no longer comes out of a furnace: it §lmelts§r, is §lcast§r into ingots (the storage form), then §lforged§r.
1. §6Fire starter§r (3 sticks + 2 plant fibers): hold right-click 2 s on a campfire, a charcoal pit, a forge hearth; 32 uses.
2. Unfired §6molds§r at the potter's bench (clay: nugget 1, ingot, plate or rod 2, gear 3), fired in the §lpottery kiln§r. A mold lasts 128 pours. No more tool-head molds: tools are forged.
3. §6Clay crucible§r on the fire, §6crucible tongs§r, placed mold: the ingot (next page).
4. §6Forge hearth§r, §6iron anvil§r (cast in an §lanvil mold§r), §lquench§r: the tool head, then assembled at the toolmaker's bench.
Plates, rods, gears and anvils are cast; wire, heads and blades are forged.

pages.title: Melting and casting
pages.text:
Set the fired §6clay crucible§r on a §llit campfire§r and feed it metal with right-click: ore (fragments, raw, crushed, dust) or ingots. It holds §l2 ingots§r (288 mB) and lasts 256 melts.
§lHeat§r: the campfire gives 1,100 °C, charcoal at its foot +100 °C, bellows up to +500 °C (§6hand bellows§r against the fire: each click a +40 °C puff that fades; or the mechanical bellows). Melting points: tin 232 °C, lead 327, zinc 420, brass 930, bronze 950, gold 1,064, copper 1,085: the fire is enough; §liron 1,538 °C: you must blow air§r. Steel does not melt in a crucible (blast furnace).
Metals mix: copper + tin = bronze, copper + zinc = brass, tin + lead = solder.
§6Crucible tongs§r (toolmaker's bench, knife: 2 rods, 2 bindings, 1 leather): right-click the crucible, you carry it with its metal; it sets in about two minutes. Right-click a §lplaced mold§r (a fired mold is placed like a block): it takes its amount; the part sets in 5 s (nugget), 10 s (ingot, plate, rods), 15 s (gear), then right-click with an empty hand. Putting the tongs back on the fire sets the crucible down; 128 pours per pair of tongs. The gear (4 ingots) needs the crucible furnace.

pages.title: Hearth and anvil
pages.text:
The §6forge hearth§r (stones, clay, a fired crucible) burns charcoal, with bellows. An ingot laid in its embers heats up to its §lworking temperature§r, without melting: copper 500 °C, brass 550, bronze 600, iron 800, steel 900. Out comes a §6heated ingot§r, glowing and cooling in the air; above 400 °C it §lburns your hand§r: hold crucible tongs in the other hand. §lRight-click§r, whatever you hold, opens the hearth's screen — that is the only place (besides hoppers) to load ingots and charcoal and to take the piece back: heat, current piece and two settings, the number of ingots (1 to 16) and of charcoal (1 to 64) it accepts. §lShift + right-click§r with flint and steel, a fire charge, matches or a torch lights it (the fire starter: hold right-click).
§6Anvil§r: just one, the §liron anvil§r (copper, tin, lead, zinc, gold, solder, bronze, brass, iron, steel). It is §lcast§r: an unfired §6anvil mold§r at the potter (knife, 8 clay), fired in the pottery kiln or on a campfire, placed on the ground (one block tall); pour 10 molten iron ingots (1,440 mB) into it with the tongs, in as many pours as needed: the metal waits for the rest. The mold refuses any other metal. Once set, take the anvil with an empty hand. Heated ingot on it, §lhammer in hand§r: the forging screen.
§6Tool rack§r (grid: 3 sticks, 2 planks, 3 slabs): 3 tools hung and on show; right-click with a tool to hang it, empty-handed to take it back.
• The chosen shape shows as a ghost on a 16 × 16 grid; one ingot = 32 pixels of material.
• §lHit§r (left click) pushes a pixel to the next cell; §ldraw§r (Shift + left click) lengthens the row; §lcut§r (right click) removes a pixel: 4 pixels of scrap = 1 nugget.
• The piece loses heat with every blow; below its working temperature nothing moves: back to the hearth, the work is kept.
• Exact shape: the §lhot part§r. Cleanly forged by hand: “Hand-forged”, +10% durability.

pages.title: Quenching and automation
Pottery and foundry
pages.text:
The foundry §lin series§r, once the crucible on the campfire is not enough. The §6pottery kiln§r (bricks and smooth stone, no vanilla furnace; 1.0.4: it is the door of a small structure of bricks, brick stairs and a brick slab, see the blueprint) fires unfired ware in bulk (molds, fire bricks, crucibles) and turns calcite into §lquicklime§r, around 900 °C. Once formed it takes its §lfinished look§r (cast-iron plinth, stone copings, chimney with an open flue where the smoke comes out) and all its masonry glows §lone single shade§r as it heats; taken apart, it gives back its bricks, stairs and slab.

The §6crucible furnace§r (fire bricks and copper) melts metal: a crucible, fuel, 3 metal slots, 9 ingots at most (1 ingot = 144 mB). On wood it tops out at §l950 °C§r; a §6forge bellows§r facing it raises it up to §l1,600 °C§r: copper (§l1,085 °C§r) then iron (§l1,538 °C§r) melt. Steel only comes from the §lblast furnace§r: no crucible makes it (1.0.5).

A §6casting table§r against it, on any side (it turns and connects by itself), a mold on it (by hand or hopper): the furnace §lpours by itself§r as soon as the table is empty and everything has melted, or on a redstone signal; the “Pour” button stays. The part sets and comes out underneath. A clay mold lasts §l128 pours§r.

pages.title: Alloys
Making an alloy
pages.text:
§6Example: bronze from ore.§r At the fire stations (clay crucible, crucible furnace, automatic foundry), §l1 raw or crushed ore = 1 ingot§r (144 mB): so you dose ores like ingots.
1. You need §l3 copper for 1 tin§r: 3 §6raw copper§r (sifted sand, malachite outcrops, drill) and 1 §6raw tin§r (cassiterite).
2. §6Crucible furnace§r: a crucible, coal; in the §lRecipe§r slot (the filter), pick §lBronze§r. Pour in the ores, even too many: the furnace only takes copper and tin, at 3 to 1 (“waits for tin” on the screen); the rest waits in its slot.
3. Copper melts at 1,085 °C: a §6forge bellows§r facing the furnace. The screen shows 75% copper, 25% tin and “Pours: bronze 4 ingots · left: nothing”.
4. A §6casting table§r against the furnace, an ingot mold on it: 4 §lbronze ingots§r.
§6At the very start§r (clay crucible, 288 mB): a small batch, for example §l6 malachite fragments + 2 cassiterite fragments§r (36 mB each), or 12 copper nuggets + 4 tin nuggets. A nugget too many or too few is no problem: the tongs pour the alloy first, then the surplus; Shift + right-click with an empty hand on the crucible empties it into ingots and nuggets.
§6Other alloys§r: brass = 3 copper + 1 zinc; solder = 3 tin + 2 lead. The §6steam induction furnace§r makes bronze, brass and solder §lstraight into ingots§r, with no melting or casting, plus red alloy and redsteel (“The induction furnace” page); machine alloys (constantan, invar…) are made in the MKI to MKIV induction furnaces, molten ones (babbitt, duralumin, electrum…) in the industrial crucible, §lfrom ingots§r. JEI: press §lU§r on an ore or §lR§r on a molten metal, “§lAlloys§r” page: proportions, ores, machines (hover: how).

pages.title: The automatic foundry
pages.text:
When the §6crucible furnace§r and the casting table can no longer keep up, the §6automatic foundry§r melts and pours §lby itself§r. A multiblock in three sizes, the same metals as the crucible furnace; only capacity and speed change:
• §l1×1×2§r: the firebox door, a vat on top — 9 ingots;
• §l2×2×3§r: 4 fireboxes (the door among them), 2 vat levels — 36 ingots, ×2;
• §l3×3×5§r (Guillaume's shape): the door, 7 fireboxes and a §6tuyere§r in the middle of the back, 4 vat levels — 144 ingots, ×4; a bellows facing the tuyere blows into the whole hearth.
The door goes on the front row, facing out (Shift + right-click with an empty hand: the blueprint). The vat glows as the metal melts.

The §6fire brick firebox§r burns §lcoal, charcoal or coke§r (coke runs hottest): on its own it tops out around 950 °C, a §6bellows§r facing a firebox raises it to 1,600 °C (iron melts). Hoppers and logistic cables feed the foundry through any part: fuel goes to the firebox, metal to the melting slots. The §lRecipe§r slot picks the alloy, as on the crucible furnace: it doses its metals and pours only that; with no choice, it waits until everything has melted, then pours as much alloy as it can and keeps the surplus (screen: “Pours … · left …”; the §lEmpty§r button as a last resort).

§6Casting channels§r against the vat, §6automatic molds§r under their spouts: the metal flows to the §lfirst free mold§r (the closest along the channels), then the next one, like a chain. In the mold's screen you pick the shape (ingot, nugget, plate, rods, gear, iron anvil); the metal sets (tin fast, iron slowly) and the part comes out underneath or on the sides, into a hopper. An automatic mold never wears out. A redstone signal on the door, or the “Auto” switch, pauses pouring.

pages.title: The blast furnace
pages.text:
Tip: §lShift + right-click with an empty hand on a controller§r (firebox, drill, tap hole) shows its structure blueprint. Guillaume's shape (1.0.4): a round §lplinth§r of §6fire brick fireboxes§r (the hearth), the §6tap hole§r — a full block — in the middle of the front and §lone§r §6tuyere§r in the middle of the back (the bellows goes behind it, facing it); above, a §6fire brick§r tower hollow in the middle, tapering into a chimney up to the throat. Once formed, the furnace gets iron hoops, its bricks glow with the heat and its fireboxes light up; you can see the charge sink and flames rise at the throat.

Throw the charge in from the top, or put it in its §lthree slots§r (one per role, hoppers and cables included): §liron§r (ore, crushed, dust, fragments, ingots), §lcarbon§r (charcoal, coal, their blocks), §lflux§r (quicklime). Blow into the tuyere: one bellows (or a steam blower) → 1,650 °C; without wind, charcoal alone does not melt steel. Above §l1,500 °C§r, steel flows, §lone ingot every 40 seconds§r; without lime, a quarter goes to slag. Careful: you §lget burned§r stepping inside a lit furnace (blast furnace, coke oven) or walking on a foundry's molten bath. Steel opens steel boilers and logistic cables (gas channel), then the Industrial Age §lcoke oven§r and industrial power hammer (hot forging).

pages.title: Forge and hardened steel
pages.text:
The §6industrial power hammer (hot forging)§r (a multiblock whose core is a §6forge hearth§r) turns a steel ingot into a §lglowing bloom§r (1,100 °C). A cooled bloom can also be reheated on a plain forge hearth, with a §6bellows§r facing it.

Plunged into water or quench oil (§6industrial furnace (heat treatment)§r), it gives §lhardened steel§r; a pass in the §6induction furnace§r (tempering) makes §ltempered steel§r. Tool heads are no longer cut cold: steel ones are forged on the iron anvil, and the §6industrial power hammer (hot forging)§r (multiblock) forges them §lcontinuously§r (ingot, hot part, built-in quench) — the only source of §lhardened steel§r heads.

The §6coke oven§r bakes coal into §lcoke§r with no fuel; §lcreosote§r drains into its tank (coal tar and coke oven gas come from the §6pyrolysis oven§r). It also chars §llogs§r: charcoal and §lcreosote§r.

pages.title: Rotation
pages.text:
Linked parts form a §6network§r turning at a §lspeed§r (rpm) under a §ltorque§r (N·m); power is their product. Sources give torque that drops as they speed up; machines ask for a fixed amount. If demand exceeds supply, everything §lstalls§r.

• §6Shafts§r: in a straight line; a §6cover frame§r fits around one (right-click), then a §lfull block§r (stone, planks…) on the frame covers it, it still turns inside; the file removes the cover then the frame (breaking too, in that order).
• Neighboring §6cogs§r: same speed, opposite way.
• §6Cogwheel§r and cog §ldiagonally§r: the cog turns twice as fast (half the torque).
• A gear only shows an §laxle§r on the side of a shaft (or part) plugged into its axis. A §6cover frame§r put on it (right-click) mounts it on a §lpivot§r: the axle is §lcut§r, meshing with its neighbors stays; the file removes the frame.
• §6Gearbox§r: changes direction.
Every part has a §lmax torque§r (wood 3,000 N·m, iron 12,000): beyond that it breaks after 2 s. §lSneak + right-click with a wrench§r: the part's sheet (speed, torque, network load).

pages.title: Tuning the drive
pages.text:
• §6Gearshift§r: right-click, a §lslider§r picks the ratio from ×¼ to ×4 (the wrench steps to the next one); a redstone signal gives direct drive.
• §6Clutch§r and §6reverser§r: a signal cuts or reverses the output.
• §6Flywheel§r: stores momentum, smooths the jolts of a horse mill or windmill.
• §6Flyball governor§r: right-click, a §lslider§r sets the target speed from 5 to 120 rpm; above it, it brakes and emits a signal (to stop a windmill in a gale); the excess turns into heat. Set to the minimum, it works as a brake.
• §6Tachometer§r and §6dynamometer§r: dials (turned toward you when placed) and comparator.

pages.title: Power sources
pages.text:
• §6Hand crank§r: hold right-click, ~90 W, makes you hungry. Too weak alone for a millstone: gear it down.
• §6Horse mill§r: bring a leashed animal and click; it walks a radius of 3 (horse, camel, mule, donkey, cow, llama). A nearby §6trough§r (wheat, hay) feeds it.
• §6Water wheel§r (3 or 5 blocks): flowing water against its paddles; a waterfall on one side is worth 2.5 times more.
• §6Windmill§r: 4 or 8 sails (canvas or planks), 3 to 7 blocks long, clear plane. Wind grows with height and changes with the weather; storms tear canvas. 1 to 20 kW.
• §6Weather vane§r: measures the wind here.

pages.title: Ropes, pulleys, winch
pages.text:
Two §6pulleys§r with parallel axes link with a rope: click one then the other (§lsneak§r: crossed strands, reversed). Up to 24 blocks, unobstructed. They may be §loffset along the axis§r: 2 blocks at most, and no more than half their spacing (the rope runs at a slant). The §lradius ratio§r (1, 2 or 3) sets the speed.
• §6Fiber rope§r: 800 N·m, 92%; §6tarred rope§r (creosote): 2,000 N·m, wears little; §6leather belt§r: 4,000 N·m, 95%.
Too much torque: it §lslips§r, wears, then snaps.

The §6winch§r reads what lies below (48 blocks at most): §lwater§r makes it a §lwell§r — each trip brings up 1,000 mB, taken by a pipe or bucket; a §lchest§r at the bottom makes it a §llift§r — the cage brings 16 items up into the chest on top of the winch. It works in both directions of rotation.

pages.title: The machines
pages.text:
Each machine needs some §ltorque§r and has a §lrated speed§r: below the minimum it stops, above the rated speed it no longer speeds up. Its screen shows the dial, the torque gauge and progress; a recipe lasts a number of §lshaft turns§r (shown in JEI).
• §6Millstone§r (vertical shaft, from below): flour, bone meal, flint dust, sugar, dyes, metal dusts.
• §6Shaking sifter§r: the hand sieve, nonstop, rope screen built in (best-mesh yield, nothing to add).
• §6Jaw crusher§r: oak frame, swing jaw on an eccentric and toggle, two flywheels: stone → gravel → sand, basalt → black sand, raw ore → crushed. Heavy torque (480 N·m).
• §6Mechanical saw§r: 6 planks per log plus sawdust (fuel).

pages.title: The machines (cont.)
pages.text:
• §6Wood lathe§r: sticks, drive shafts (8 per log), bowls, metal rods, rings and springs.
• §6Forge bellows§r: facing a hearth, a furnace or a blast furnace, it smelts §ltwice as fast§r.
• §6Noria§r: placed above water, it lifts one source per second into the block above, or into the tank there.
• §6Wooden fluid buffer§r: a barrel of staves with iron hoops, 8,000 mB of cold fluid; placed on the noria, it connects to it and collects its water.
Outputs empty through the faces (hopper, chest, logistic cable).

pages.title: Drill, hopper and placing
pages.text:
• §6Mechanical drill§r: placed on rock, it draws stone from it without wearing it down — §lcobblestone§r from stone, granite from granite, and so on. One block every §l3 turns§r (about 13 a minute at 40 rpm), 240 N·m. It pushes its blocks into a neighboring container (chest, wooden hopper), otherwise keeps them in its slot.
• §6Wooden hopper§r: §lno inventory§r. Twice a second it takes one item from above (container or dropped item) and puts it straight into the container its spout points at; whatever is poured in goes straight through. Redstone signal: stop.

§lPlacing parts§r: a shaft clicked on the side of a shaft extends the line at its end (on the side you look toward); a cogwheel clicked on the rim of a cog, or the reverse, goes §ldiagonally§r, where it meshes — a golden frame shows the spot. The axis chosen is the one that connects to the neighbors. §lSneak§r: free placement, along your gaze.

pages.title: The beam engine
pages.text:
The first steam engine, peak of the Mechanical Age. A brick boiler under a rocking beam: fill it with §lwater§r (buckets or pipe) and §lfuel§r, wait for the water to boil (373 K): steam comes up, full around §l403 K§r.

Starting torque up to §l9,000 N·m§r, 14 rpm unloaded: enough to drive a whole line of crushers and saws. Water evaporates in step with the power delivered; §ldry§r, the boiler overheats and goes out. The shaft comes out of the left side, under the flywheel.

pages.title: The boiler
pages.text:
A fixed structure (Shift + right-click the firebox with an empty hand: the blueprint; 1.0.4, Guillaume's shape): the §6firebox§r in the middle of the front, 4 §6fire brick fireboxes§r in a cross behind it; above, 11 §6boiler shells§r (two levels of 5 in a cross and one in the center, 4,000 mB of water each); the §6steam dome§r in front of the top shell, as the outlet (copper-colored on copper, gray on steel); a §6chimney§r of 1 to 8 blocks on the top shell — the taller, the better the draft; an optional §6water gauge§r. Water by bucket, through a pipe (logistic cable) or with the §6injector§r.

Steam is a §lquantity§r: water boils at 100 °C (1 mB of water → 8 mB of steam) and steam builds up in the parts' §lreserve§r (copper shell 12,000 mB, steel shell 32,000 mB, dome 8,000 mB). With the reserve full, the fire keeps going and the boiler stays at 100 °C: the surplus steam escapes through the valve (“surplus lost”), nothing breaks. Draft ×0.4 without a chimney, +0.15 per block, ×1.6 at 8 blocks: from §l7 mB/t§r (one-block chimney) to §l29 mB/t§r with wood, up to §l50 mB/t§r with coal (+60%). The chimney makes the fuel burn faster, with no loss: a fuel item always gives the same steam (coal ≈ 54,000 mB). Every figure: JEI page “Steam Boiler”.
§lThe only danger§r: firing it §lwithout water§r. Water below 15% → alarm; no water left with the fire lit → the metal glows red, then the boiler §lblows up§r; cold water on red-hot metal → thermal shock. Overfilled (> 92%) → wet steam, machines at half power.

pages.title: Conduits and fittings
Steam machines
pages.text:
§6Steam engine§r: steam from the back or below, shaft on the sides; §l12,000 N·m§r starting torque, 120 rpm unloaded, §l0.48 mB/t of steam per rpm§r (29 mB/t at 60 rpm, ~1,900 FE/t through a dynamo: one well-drafted boiler per engine). Spent steam leaves through the exhaust (front): keep the boiler filled with a cable or a bucket.

The §6blower§r blows into a furnace or tuyere like three bellows, for 17 mB/t. The §6steam hammer§r is gone (1.0.5): a steam hammer already placed becomes a §lsteam saw§r and drops its materials on the ground; stone cutting is done at the saw, the mason's mixes at the mixer. The §6steam press§r is a processing machine: it §lflattens§r (next page).

pages.title: Steam factory
The induction furnace
Tiers and families
pages.text:
Every processing machine has a §6tier§r and a §6family§r (grinding, sifting, sawing, turning, compacting, extraction, smelting, rolling, wire drawing, mixing, pressing, hammering, induction). Scale: §lT0 mechanical§r, §lT1 bronze§r (steam), §lT2 MKI§r, T3 MKII, T4 MKIII, T5 MKIV.
• A machine makes §levery recipe of its family up to its tier§r: the steam macerator (T1) makes those of the millstone and the jaw crusher (T0); the MKI crusher (T2), those of all three.
• Each tier above the recipe's tier: §ltwice as fast§r.
• §lRaw materials§r (raw ore, logs, plants…) yield more: ×1.5 at T1, ×1.75 at T2, ×2.19 at T3, ×2.63 at T4, ×3.5 at T5 (for a T0 recipe). Raw ore → crushed stops at T1 (3 crushed): higher up, the gain comes from the industrial crucible. Never on metal forms (dust, plate, rod, bolt…): no machine creates metal.
• Several recipes for the same input: the highest-tier one wins; the §lselector§r locks one.
• The steam machine also makes the §lopened MKI recipes§r of its family, twice as slowly as MKI (“MKI recipes by steam” page).
The tier shows on the interface (T0 to T5 chip), in the tooltip (“Tier 1 — Bronze · Grinding family”) and in JEI (“Min. tier”).

pages.title: MKI recipes by steam
pages.text:
Each steam machine also makes part of the §6MKI recipes§r of its family: §l131 recipes§r (compacting 44, smelting 18, rolling 17, sawing 12, grinding 12, wire drawing 11, sifting 8, mixing 5, turning 4). Same inputs, same outputs, same steam per tick, but §ltwice as slow§r as on the MKI machine, which stays faster and keeps its ore yields.
• Kept for MKI: anything that uses an MKI-age material or later (steel, brass, nickel, aluminum…, ores from deep deposits), the key MKI components and milestones, recipes with fluids, gases or heat, ore yields, bench copies (in the Bronze Age benches stay manual) and anything that would bring MKI earlier.
• With no lock, the machine makes its own recipes first; the §lselector§r then offers the opened MKI recipes (screen: “Recipe: MKI · speed ×½”).
JEI shows them on the page of the family's §lMKI machine§r, with the MKI duration (twice as long by steam).

pages.title: Concrete and the steam mixer
pages.text:
§lLight gray concrete§r is the basic concrete. At the §6mason's bench§r: §l4 sand + 4 gravel + 1 quicklime → 8 light gray concrete powder§r; §l8 light gray powder + 1 dye → 8 powder§r of that color. Powder placed in water sets into concrete, as always.
To make a lot of it, the §6steam mixer§r (at the crafting table like the other steam machines: bronze plates and gears, a bronze cable, a cauldron in the middle, iron plates): 4 input slots and an §l8-bucket water tank§r (bucket by right-click, cable, pump):
• §l4 gravel + 4 sand + 1 quicklime (+ 1 dye) + 1 bucket of water → 8 concrete§r in 8 s;
• without water: the §l8 powder§r; §l8 powder + 1 bucket of water → 8 concrete§r.
It tries the most complete recipe first (with dye, with water). In the Industrial Age the §6mixer§r makes all 16 concretes with cement, and powder with water.

pages.title: Prospecting and drilling
pages.text:
